about.title: About the project
about.intro: Fortune Platform open-sources the Manseryeok (Korean Four Pillars calendar) engine refined in a production Saju AI service. It runs entirely with plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript — no backend — and is hosted for free on GitHub Pages. It provides accurate calculations only, with no AI interpretation.
features: Precise lunar calendar conversion for 1900–2100 (incl. leap months)
Year/month pillars decided by exact solar-term times (minute precision)
Stems & branches, five elements, hidden stems, Ten Gods, 12 life stages, void branches
Napeum (納音) elements for all 60 cycle pairs
DST, historical Korean standard time, yajasi option, multi-timezone
Western natal chart (10 planets, ASC/MC, aspects)
tech: Frontend: plain HTML5 + CSS3 + JavaScript (ES6 modules)
Backend: none — everything is computed in the browser
about.dataText: Calendar data (solar-term times and the lunar table, 1900–2100) was extracted from a reference Manseryeok database and cross-verified across all 73,000+ days; gaps were recomputed with the NASA JPL DE421 ephemeris. Astrology uses a public-domain low-precision algorithm whose error against the JPL ephemeris is enforced by tests (see the test/ directory).
about.licenseText: This project is distributed under the MIT License. You are free to use, modify and redistribute it.
about.contributeText: Bug reports, data corrections and feature ideas are all welcome — please open a GitHub issue or pull request.

guide.title: Complete Saju Manseryeok Guide
guide.intro: Key concepts for understanding a Korean Four Pillars chart: heavenly stems and earthly branches, the five elements, solar terms and the month branch, and Napeum elements.
guide.s1t: What are Heavenly Stems and Earthly Branches?
guide.s1p: The stems and branches form the traditional East Asian time-reckoning system. Ten heavenly stems combine with twelve earthly branches into a cycle of sixty pairs (the sexagenary cycle). A Saju chart expresses the year, month, day and hour of birth as four such pairs — eight characters in total, hence 'Saju Palja' (four pillars, eight characters).
guide.s2p: The five elements are Wood, Fire, Earth, Metal and Water. Every stem and branch carries an element and a yin/yang polarity, and the distribution of elements across the eight characters is the starting point of traditional analysis. This calculator tallies the distribution automatically.
guide.s3t: Solar terms and the month branch (Wolryeong)
guide.s3p: The year and month pillars change not at calendar boundaries but at solar-term moments determined by the sun's position. The year pillar changes at Ipchun (start of spring); each month pillar changes at its 'Jeol' term. Someone born before Ipchun uses the previous year's pillar. The month branch (Wolryeong) represents the seasonal energy of the whole chart. This calculator compares term times to the minute.
guide.s4p: Napeum assigns a poetic elemental name to each pair of the sixty cycle — for example Gapja/Eulchuk are 'Gold in the Sea' (海中金) and Byeongin/Jeongmyo are 'Fire in the Furnace' (爐中火). Traditional Manseryeok almanacs print the Napeum of each pillar.
guide.s5t: Hidden stems, Ten Gods and the 12 stages
guide.s5p: Hidden stems (Jijanggan) are the stems concealed within each branch. The Ten Gods classify every other character relative to the day master (the day stem) into ten relations. The 12 life stages express the day master's strength cycle (Birth through Nurture) at each branch.
guide.s6p: Daeun are 10-year luck cycles that proceed forward or backward from the month pillar (forward for yang-year males and yin-year females). The starting age is the day count to the nearest Jeol term divided by three. For accurate hour pillars the calculator supports the Korean −30 minute longitude adjustment, Korean DST periods (1948–1960, 1987–1988), and the historical UTC+8:30 standard time (1908–1911, 1954–1961).

items.q: How is the Saju chart calculated?
items.a: From your birth date and time the app converts lunar dates if needed, compares exact solar-term times, and derives the four pillars. Everything is computed instantly in your browser.

items.q: Why does the birth time matter?
items.a: The time determines the hour pillar, and births after 23:00 can even shift the day pillar. If you don't know it, choose 'Time unknown' — the chart shows three pillars.

items.q: Can I enter a lunar birthday?
items.a: Yes. Switch the calendar to 'Lunar' and the app converts it precisely to a solar date within 1900–2100, including leap months.

items.q: How do I enter a leap-month birth?
items.a: Select 'Lunar' and tick the 'Leap month' checkbox. If that year has no such leap month you'll get an error message.

items.q: What about births near a term boundary such as Ipchun?
items.a: Pillars are decided by the exact term moment (to the minute), not the date. Born on Ipchun day but before the Ipchun time? The previous year's pillar is used.

items.q: What is the Korean −30 minute adjustment?
items.a: Korea's standard meridian is 135°E but Seoul lies near 127°E, so solar time runs about 30 minutes behind the clock. By convention the two-hour blocks are shifted 30 minutes later. It is on by default for Korean births.

items.q: Are DST and historical standard time handled?
items.a: Yes. Korean DST periods (1948–1960, 1987–1988) subtract one hour automatically, and the UTC+8:30 standard-time eras (1908–1911, 1954–1961) are reflected. For other countries use the manual DST checkbox.

items.q: What is the yajasi (late Rat hour) rule?
items.a: By default, births after 23:00 belong to the next day's Rat hour. The yajasi convention keeps them on the same day instead. You can toggle it in the advanced options; schools differ on this.

items.q: Are the tarot and astrology results interpretations?
items.a: No. Tarot shows traditional card keywords and astrology shows computed celestial positions. This project deliberately contains no AI interpretation or divinatory advice.
No. There is no backend server; everything you enter is processed only inside your browser and never transmitted or stored.
